verses.zh: 耶和华的话临到我说：
verses.en: (21:6)[NOTE:1] The Lord’s message came to me:
notes: Ezek 21:1 in the English Bible is 21:6 in the Hebrew text (BHS). See the note at 20:45.
verses.commentary:
21:1 The context starts in Ezek. 20:45, which marks off a new vision by the characteristic phrase "the word of the Lord
came to me saying" (cf. Ezek. 3:16; 6:1; 7:1; 11:14; 12:1,8,17, 21,26; 13:1; 14:2,12; 15:1; 16:1; 17:1,11; 18:1; 20:2,45; 21:1,8,18; 22:1,17,23; 23:1;
24:1,15,20; 25:1; 26:1; 27:1; 28:1,7; 30:1,20; 31:1; 32:1,17; 33:1,23; 34:1; 35:1; 36:16; 38:1). Remember that the original manuscripts had no chapters, paragraphs,
or verse divisions in the ancient Hebrew scrolls. This repeated phrase helped scroll readers find the place to begin reading. It also helped to show (1) new contexts and (2) related contexts.

Special Topic: Names for Deity, D.

▣ "saying" This VERB (BDB 55, KB 65) occurs twenty-two times in this
chapter. YHWH wants His wayward people to hear Him clearly!

verses.zh: 「人子啊，你要面向耶路撒冷和圣所滴下预言，攻击以色列地。
verses.en: “Son of man, turn toward[NOTE:1] Jerusalem[NOTE:2] and speak out against the sanctuaries. Prophesy against the land of Israel
notes: Heb “set your face toward.”
For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.
verses.commentary:
21:2 "Son of man" See note at Ezek. 2:1.

Special Topic: Son of Man

▣ "set your face toward Jerusalem" This is judgment imagery. Notice it says, "the land of Israel," but it denotes Judah.
Israel is already in exile in Assyria. See note at Ezek. 20:41.

▣ Notice the negative parallelism.

- Set your face toward (BDB 962, KB 1321, Qal IMPERATIVE)

- Speak against (lit. "preach," BDB 642, KB 694, Hiphil IMPERATIVE)

- Prophesy against (BDB 612, KB 659, Niphal IMPERATIVE)

This exactly matches Ezek. 20:46. YHWH's judgment against His own disobedient people is described by the
personification of His sharp (BDB 292) and polished (BDB 598) sword.

His sword will strike

- the capital with its political leaders

- the mountain/hilltop sanctuaries of Ba'al and Asherah

- the entire Promised Land

verses.zh: 对以色列地说，耶和华如此说：我与你为敌，并要拔刀出鞘，从你中间将义人和恶人一并剪除。
verses.en: and say to them,[NOTE:1] ‘This is what the Lord says: Look,[NOTE:2] I am against you.[NOTE:3] I will draw my sword[NOTE:4] from its sheath and cut off from you both the righteous and the wicked.[NOTE:5]
notes: Heb “the land of Israel.”
The word הִנֵּה (hinneh, traditionally “behold”) draws attention to something and has been translated here as a verb.

Or “I challenge you.” The phrase “I am against you” may be a formula for challenging someone to combat or a duel. See D. I. Block, Ezekiel (NICOT), 1:201-2, and P. Humbert, “Die Herausforderungsformel ‘hinnenî ’êlékâ’” ZAW 45 (1933): 101-8.
This is the sword of judgment; see Isa 31:8; 34:6; 66:16.

Ezekiel elsewhere pictures the Lord’s judgment as discriminating between the righteous and the wicked (9:4-6; 18:1-20; see as well Pss 1 and 11) and speaks of the preservation of a remnant (3:21; 6:8; 12:16). Perhaps here he exaggerates for rhetorical effect in an effort to subdue any false optimism. See L. C. Allen, Ezekiel (WBC), 2:25-26; D. I. Block, Ezekiel (NICOT), 1:669-70; and W. Zimmerli, Ezekiel (Hermeneia), 1:424-25. The words do not require all the people in each category to be cut off.
verses.commentary:
21:3 "sword" This is one of the most graphic chapters in all of the Bible on the judgment of YHWH. YHWH's sword
(BDB 352, cf. Ezek. 21:3,4, 5,9,2,14,15,19; Isa. 31:8; 34:6; 66:16) is personified and His attitude of judgment is heightened.
In Ezek. 20:49 (MT 21:5) the leadership in exile said, "Don't speak to us in parables anymore," so Ezekiel graphically described
the judgment of YHWH on Jerusalem and Judah (cf. Jer. 12:12).

21:3-4 "cut off from you the righteous and the wicked" In Ezek. 20:47 the same groups are described as green and dry
trees. YHWH's judgment on those left in Judah will affect both the faithful and unfaithful (see Special Topic: Biblical Faith is Corporate).
The Septuagint changes the term "righteous" to the term "unrighteous" because they think this verse violates the truth presented in
Ezek. 14:20; 18:lff; 33:lff (see Hard Sayings of the Bible, pp. 315-316). Isaiah 57:1-2 struggles with this issue and gives an after-life answer.

Special Topic: Septuagint

verses.zh: 我既要从你中间剪除义人和恶人，所以我的刀要出鞘，自南至北攻击一切有血气的；
verses.en: Because I will cut off from you both the righteous and the wicked, my sword will go out from its sheath against everyone[NOTE:1] from the south[NOTE:2] to the north.
notes: Heb “all flesh” (also in the following verse).
Heb “Negev.” The Negev is the south country.

verses.zh: 一切有血气的就知道我―耶和华已经拔刀出鞘，必不再入鞘。
verses.en: Then everyone will know that I am the Lord, who drew my sword from its sheath—it will not be sheathed again!’
verses.commentary:
21:5 "Thus all flesh will know that I, the Lord" This "all flesh" (cf.
Ezek. 20:48; 21:4,5) emphasis can be seen in two aspects.

- all humans, Num. 16:22; 27:16; Ezek. 20:48 (i.e. Gen. 1:26-27, possibly eschatological)

- all Judah, Ezek. 21:4,5; Jer. 12:12 (immediate context)

YHWH cares about His namesake among the nations (cf. Ezek. 36:22-38). The seed of Abraham was YHWH's
instrument to reach the nations (i.e. Gen. 12:3).

Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

▣ "It will not return to its sheath again" This is an idiom for YHWH's judgment that
cannot be stopped (cf. Jer. 23:20). It seems to contrast Ezek. 21:30. This is literary hyperbole. Judgment
was sure (cf. Ezek. 21:7)! Those left in Jerusalem did not believe judgment was truly coming, not to
Jerusalem, not to the temple, not to them! They misunderstood YHWH's longsuffering, patient endurance.

verses.zh: 人子啊，你要叹息，在他们眼前弯着腰，苦苦地叹息。
verses.en: “And you, son of man, groan with an aching heart[NOTE:1] and bitterness; groan before their eyes.
notes: Heb “breaking loins.”
verses.commentary:
21:6 "groan with breaking heart" This VERB (BDB 58, KB 70) is used twice.

- Niphal IMPERATIVE (command)

- Niphal IMPERFECT (continuing action)

This VERB denotes a deep distress caused by physical or emotional pain
(i.e. Lam. 1:8,22). In Ezek. 9:4 it is used to describe the guilt feelings connected to true repentance
(note Jer. 13:17).

"Heart" is literally "loins" (BDB 608). This was the seat of strength (i.e. the largest muscle
in the body is the thigh). It is a Hebrew idiom (cf. Ezek. 21:12; Job 40:16; Ps. 66:11; Isa. 21:3; Nahum 2:10).
Verse 6 describes another symbolic drama dictated by YHWH for the purpose of reaching exiled Judah.

verses.zh: 他们问你说：『为何叹息呢？』你就说：『因为有风声、灾祸要来。人心都必消化，手都发软，精神衰败，膝弱如水。看哪，这灾祸临近，必然成就。这是主耶和华说的。』」
verses.en: When they ask you, ‘Why are you groaning?’ you will reply, ‘Because of the report that has come. Every heart will melt with fear and every hand will be limp; everyone[NOTE:1] will faint, and every knee will be wet with urine.’[NOTE:2] Pay attention—it is coming and it will happen, declares the Sovereign Lord.”
notes: Heb “every spirit will be dim.”
This expression depicts in a very vivid way how they will be overcome with fear. See the note on the same phrase in 7:17.
verses.commentary:
21:7 Note the reason for groaning was the arrival of YHWH's sword.

- every heart will melt

- every hand will be feeble

- all hands will be feeble

- every spirit will faint

- all knees will be weak as water (i.e. possibly referring to urinating on oneself in fear)

This description of utter fear and desperation is used to describe YHWH's judgment on the
pagan nations.

- Canaan, Josh. 2:11; 5:1

- Babylon, Isa. 13:7; Jer. 50:43

- Egypt, Isa. 19:1

- Assyria, Nah. 2:10

- Syria, Jer. 49:24

- on the wicked, Ezek. 7:17

But now on Judah (i.e. Lev. 26 and Deut. 28 are a reality).

verses.zh: 耶和华的话临到我说：
verses.en: The Lord’s message came to me:

verses.zh: 「人子啊，你要预言。耶和华吩咐我如此说：有刀、有刀，是磨快擦亮的；
verses.en: “Son of man, prophesy and say: ‘This is what the Lord says:“‘A sword, a sword is sharpenedand also polished.
verses.commentary:
21:9 The urgency of the message is stressed, as it was in Ezek. 21:2. This verse has

- two IMPERTIVES

- "prophesy," BDB 612, KB 659, Niphal IMPERATIVE

- "say," BDB 55, KB 65, Qal IMPERATIVE

- "say" repeated several times

- "saying," Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT, Ezek. 21:8

- "say," Qal PERFECT, Ezek. 21:9

- "say," Qal PERFECT, Ezek. 21:9

- "say," Qal IMPERATIVE, Ezek. 21:9

verses.zh: 磨快为要行杀戮，擦亮为要像闪电。我们岂可快乐吗？罚我子的杖藐视各树。
verses.en: It is sharpened for slaughter; it is polished to flash like lightning!“‘Should we rejoice in the scepter of my son? No! The sword despises every tree![NOTE:1]
notes: The people of Judah should not place false hope in their king, symbolized by his royal scepter, for God’s judgment (symbolized by fire and then a sword) would destroy every tree (see 20:47), symbolizing the righteous and wicked (see 21:3-4). tn Heb “Or shall we rejoice, scepter of my son? It despises every tree.” The translation understands the subject of the verb “despises,” which is a feminine form in the Hebrew text, to be the sword (which is a feminine noun) mentioned just before this. Alternatively, the line may be understood as “Let us not rejoice, O tribe of my son; it despises every tree.” The same word in Hebrew may be either “rod,” “scepter,” or “tribe.” The word sometimes translated as “or” or taken as an interrogative particle may be a negative particle. See D. I. Block, Ezekiel (NICOT), 1:672, n. 79.
verses.commentary:
21:10 It is often hard to tell the difference between "elevated prose" and poetry.

- NASB has Ezek. 21:9b-10a as poetry

- NKJV has Ezek. 21:9b-11,12,13,14-15,16,17,26-27, 28b-29,30-32 as poetry

- NRSV has Ezek. 21:9b-12,14-17,25-27,28b-32 as poetry

- TEV has Ezek. 21:9b-13,28b as poetry

▣ "polished to flash like lightening" This is a Hebrew idiom of both speed and turning many
directions (i.e. Nah. 2:3-4).

NASB
"Or shall we rejoice, the rod of My son despising

every tree"

NKJV
"It despises the scepter of My son, as it does

all wood"

NRSV
"How can we make merry? You have despised the

rod, and all discipline"

TEV
"There can be no rejoicing, for my people have

disregarded every warning and punishment"

LXX
ready for slaughter, slay, set at naught, despise

every tree"

Peshitta
"and it is sharpened to cut off the family of my son;

and to reject every other branch"

REB
"(Look, the rod is brandished, my son, to defy

all wooden idols)"

JPSOA
"How can we rejoice? My son, it scorns the rod

and every stick"

Obviously the Hebrew text is in disarray (note the differences in the translations, ancient and
modern).

- The mentioning of the word "rod" (BDB 986) in Ezek. 21:10,13 can refer to

- a rod of correction by a parent (cf. Prov. 10:13; 22:15)

- a rod for correction by a community (cf. Prov. 19:29; 26:3)

- a staff of a shepherd

- a scepter of a king

- a club of a shepherd (Ps. 23:4)

- a means of divine punishment (Ezek. 21:10)

Here in Ezek. 21:10, it may refer to

- Zedekiah's impotence in protecting Judah from Neo-Babylonian invasion, in which every
Judean left in the land will be affected (i.e. "despising every tree," cf. Ezek. 20:47; 21:3-4)

- a future leader from the tribe of Judah (Gen. 49:10); alluded to in Ezek. 21:27

- These verses are related in the people's concept that the ancient promises of YHWH for a special leader
(i.e. "My son"), presented in Gen. 49:10 (cf. Targums, cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 4, pp. 1267-8), would be
fulfilled instead of judgment.

- The phrase "every tree" somehow refers to the total judgment of Ezek. 20:47.

- In context it seems best to see the object of the FEMININE VERB "despise,"
Ezek. 21:10,13, to refer to "the sword" of YHWH. The Jerusalemites disregarded the prophets Jeremiah
and Ezekiel's messages of judgment, but in reality the continuous Davidic line of kings from David
(cf. 2 Samuel 7) would be stopped. Zedekiah would be the last. However, one would come in the future
(cf. Ezek. 21:26b; 27b).

- UBS Text Project, p. 62, suggests the translation, "or shoud we rejoice (that) 'the scepter of my
son (i.e. of King Zedekiah) looks down upon all (other) scrptors."

YHWH states that nothing at this point could stop His judgment from falling on Jerusalem, who had
despised His prophetic messages.

verses.zh: 这刀已经交给人擦亮，为要应手使用。这刀已经磨快擦亮，好交在行杀戮的人手中。
verses.en: “‘He gave it to be polished,to be grasped in the hand—the sword is sharpened, it is polished—giving it into the hand of the executioner.
verses.commentary:
21:11 "the slayer" This term (BDB 246, KB 255, Qal PARTICIPLE) denotes
the invading mercenary army of Neo-Babylon. It is used of the judgment on Tyre in Ezek. 28:9. It is also used in
Jeremiah's description of Judah's destruction (i.e. Jer. 4:27-31).

verses.zh: 人子啊，你要呼喊哀号，因为这刀临到我的百姓和以色列一切的首领。他们和我的百姓都交在刀下，所以你要拍腿叹息。
verses.en: Cry out and moan, son of man,for it is wielded against my people,against all the princes of Israel.They are delivered up to the sword, along with my people.Therefore, strike your thigh.[NOTE:1]
notes: This physical action was part of an expression of grief. Cf. Jer 31:19.
verses.commentary:
21:12 Three IMPERATIVES related to mourning are mentioned in this verse.

- "Cry out," BDB 277, KB 277, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Ezek. 9:8; 11:13; 27:30;
Isa. 14:31; Jer. 25:34; 48:20

- "Wail" or "howl," BDB 410, KB 413, Hiphil IMPERATIVE, cf. Ezek. 30:2;
Isa. 14:31; 49:3; Jer. 25:34; 47:2; 48:20,21; Hosea 7:14; Zech. 11:2

- "Strike," BDB 706, KB 765, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Jer. 31:19

The theme of total slaughter continues as "against My people" is paralleled with "against the officials
of Israel" (cf. Ezek. 21:25; 22:6).

▣ "strike your thigh" The thigh (BDB 437) was the largest muscle in the body. To strike
one's thigh was imagery for

- incapacitation

- pain (cf. Jer. 31:19)

verses.zh: 有试验的事；若那藐视的杖归于无有，怎么样呢？这是主耶和华说的。
verses.en: “‘For testing will come, and what will happen when the scepter, which the sword despises, is no more?[NOTE:1] declares the Sovereign Lord.’
notes: Heb “For testing (will come), and what if also a scepter it despises will not be?” The translation understands the subject of the verb “despises,” which is a feminine form in the Hebrew text, to be the sword (which is a feminine noun) mentioned in the previous verses. The text is very difficult, and any rendering is uncertain.
verses.commentary:
21:13

NASB
"For there is a testing; and what if even the rod which

despises will be no more"

NKJV
"Because it is a testing and what if the sword despises

even the scepter"

NRSV
"For consider: What! If you despise the rod, will it not

happen"

TEV
"I am testing my people, and if they refuse to repent,

all these things will happen to them"

TEV
"I am testing my people, and if they refuse to repent,

all these things will happen to them"

NJB
"for this will be an ordeal"

LXX
"and what if even the tribe be rejected"

JPSOA
"Consider: How shall it fail to happen, seeing that it

even scorns the rod"

This may refer to the life and exile of King Zedekiah. He despised YHWH's leadership, now he is rejected
as leader. But one of David's line will be king again in the future (Ezek. 21:26b, 27b; 2 Sam. 7; 1 Chr. 17). This may parallel Ezek. 21:10.

verses.zh: 「人子啊，你要拍掌预言。我―耶和华要使这刀，就是致死伤的刀，一连三次加倍刺人，进入他们的内屋，使大人受死伤的就是这刀。
verses.en: “And you, son of man, prophesy, and clap your hands together.Let the sword strike twice, even three times!It is a sword for slaughter,a sword for the great slaughter surrounding them.
verses.commentary:
21:14 This verse also has several commands from YHWH to Ezekiel.

- prophesy, BDB 612, KB 659, Niphal IMPERATIVE

- "clap your hands," BDB 645, KB 697, Hiphil IMPERATIVE

- "let the sword be doubled," BDB 495, KB 493, Niphal IMPERFECT used
in a JUSSIVE sense. Doubled is imagery for a complete and total destruction.

▣ "clap your hands together" This physical gesture of clapping the hands denotes
several different emotions.

- affirmation, 2 Kgs. 11:12

- anger, Num. 24:10; Ezek. 21:14

- contempt/mockery, Job 27:23; 34:37 (possibly 36:18); Lam. 2:15; Ezek. 6:11; 25:3,6

- pledge/oath, Prov. 11:21; Ezek. 21:17

- joy, Ps. 47:1; 98:8; Isa. 55:12

If you look these up you will see there is some overlap in these categories and the exact emotion meant is often uncertain.

Special Topic: Hand

NASB, NRSV
"surrounds them"

NKJV
"enters their private chambers"

NJB
"threatening them from every side"

REB
"whirling about them"

This VERB (BDB 293, KB 293, Qal PARTICIPLE) occurs only here
in the OT. Its basic meaning in the cognate languages is

- encompass

- room, chamber

- In Sirah 51:10, it means "to enter" (i.e. "a penetrating sword," cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 28).

verses.zh: 我设立这恐吓人的刀，攻击他们的一切城门，使他们的心消化，加增他们跌倒的事。哎！这刀造得像闪电，磨得尖利，要行杀戮。
verses.en: So hearts melt with fear and many stumble.At all their gates I have stationed the sword for slaughter.Ah! It is made to flash, it is drawn for slaughter!
verses.commentary:
21:15 This is the filfillment of Ezek. 21:7. See note there.

▣ "many fall at all their gates" The gates would be the key defensive positions. Resistance was futile!

NASB, Peshitta
"the glittering sword"

NKJV
"made bright"

NRSV
"the point of the sword"

TEV, REB
"that flashes like lightning"

NJB
"polished to flash like lightning"

JPSOA
"from its sheath"

LXX
"for glittering"

The UBS Text Project, p. 63, suggests three possible meanings of this abvbiguous Hebrew phrase.

- the threat of the sword

- the unsheathing of the sword

- the glittering of the sword

verses.zh: 刀啊，你归在右边，摆在左边；你面向哪方，就向那方杀戮。
verses.en: Cut sharply on the right!Swing to[NOTE:1] the left, wherever your edge[NOTE:2] is appointed to strike.
notes: Heb “Put to.”
Heb “face.”
verses.commentary:
21:16 This verse has four Hiphil IMPERATIVES, FEMININE SINGULAR. This is another personification of YHWH's
sword. It is addressed in several IMPERATIVES.

- NASB ‒ "show yourself sharp"

NKJV ‒ "swords at the ready!"

TEV ‒ "you sharp sword!"

REB ‒ "be sharpened"

LXX ‒ "sharpen thyself"

The MT has a root, אחד (KB 29), that is unknown. Most translations emend it to חדד (BDB 292). KB
291 lists several stem connotations:

- Qal ‒ to be quick

- Hiphil ‒ to sharpen

- Hophal ‒ to be sharpened

- Hithpael ‒ to prove oneself sharp

The UBS Text Project, p. 64, gives a "C" rating to "join (in an attack)" directed to the sword.

- "Go to the right," BDB 412, KB 415, Hiphil IMPERATIVE

- "Set yourself," BDB 962, KB 1321, Hiphil IMPERATIVE

- "Go to the left," BDB 970, KB 1332, Hiphil IMPERATIVE

verses.zh: 我也要拍掌，并要使我的忿怒止息。这是我―耶和华说的。」
verses.en: I too will clap my hands together,I will exhaust my rage;I, the Lord, have spoken.”
verses.commentary:
21:17 YHWH brings the deserved judgment and He also stops it at His discretion (cf. Ezek. 5:13;
16:42; 24:13)! Judah's fall and exile are not the result of the power of the invading army (cf. Ezek. 21:19-27).

verses.zh: 耶和华的话又临到我说：
verses.en: The Lord’s message came to me:

verses.zh: 「人子啊，你要定出两条路，好使巴比伦王的刀来。这两条路必从一地分出来，又要在通城的路口上画出一只手来。
verses.en: “You, son of man, mark out two routes for the king of Babylon’s sword to take; both of them will originate in a single land. Make a signpost and put it at the beginning of the road leading to the city.
verses.commentary:
21:19-20 This is another acted-out parable at YHWH's command (BDB 962, KB 1321, Qal IMPERATIVE).
Apparently Ezekiel drew a map ("mark," "make," "appoint," BDB 962, KB 1321, Qal IMPERATIVE) in the ground.
At the fork in the road, one sign ("cut down," "cut out," "inscribe," "prepare a wooden sign" [BDB 388], BDB 135, KB 153, Piel
INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE, twice; in other TENSES this is the term for YHWH creating in Genesis 1).

- One sign at the fork pointed to Riblah, the capital of Ammon.

- The other sign at the fork pointed to Jerusalem, the capital of Judah. Ammon had also rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar II (cf. Jer. 27:1-3).

- Both of these capitals deserved and received YHWH's judgment by means of Neo-Babylon (Ezek. 21:22)!

Ezekiel is mimicking what Nebuchadnezzar, a pagan, superstitious king would do as he approached the fork in
the road. One would lead down the right side of the Jordan River and one down the left. Eventually, both capitals fell. The thrust
of the acted out parable was that YHWH would lead him to act on His behalf, not diviners but the Divine One!

verses.zh: 你要定出一条路，使刀来到亚扪人的拉巴；又要定出一条路，使刀来到犹大的坚固城耶路撒冷。
verses.en: Mark out the routes for the sword to take: ‘Rabbah of the Ammonites’ and ‘Judah with Jerusalem in it.’[NOTE:1]
notes: The MT reads “Judah in fortified Jerusalem,” a geographic impossibility. The translation follows the LXX, which assumes בְּתוֹכָהּ (betokhah, “in it”) for בְּצוּרָה (betsurah, “fortified”). sn As the Babylonians approached from the north, one road would branch off to the left and lead down the east side of the Jordan River to Ammon. The other road would veer to the right and lead down west of the Jordan to Jerusalem.

verses.zh: 因为巴比伦王站在岔路那里，在两条路口上要占卜。他摇签（原文是箭）求问神像，察看牺牲的肝；
verses.en: For the king of Babylon stands at the fork[NOTE:1] in the road at the head of the two routes. He looks for omens:[NOTE:2] He shakes arrows, he consults idols,[NOTE:3] he examines[NOTE:4] animal livers.[NOTE:5]
notes: Heb “mother.”

Mesopotamian kings believed that the gods revealed the future through omens. They employed various divination techniques, some of which are included in the list that follows. A particularly popular technique was the examination and interpretation of the livers of animals. See R. R. Wilson, Prophecy and Society in Ancient Israel, 90-110.
This word refers to personal idols that were apparently used for divination purposes (Gen 31:19; 1 Sam 19:13, 16).
Heb “sees.”
Heb “the liver.”
verses.commentary:
21:21 This verse describes three Babylonian means of knowing the will of the gods by divination.

- putting the names on arrows and drawing one out (or spinning the quiver until one fell out) of the quiver
or throwing arrows on the ground and analyzing their patterns

- consulting the household idols or ancestral spirits by prayer and incense (i.e. teraphim,
cf. Gen. 31:19ff; see
Special Topic: Teraphim)

- examining a sheep's liver for signs (i.e. color, shape, deformities; see Special Topic: Divination)

God is asserting that even by means of pagan divination He will bring judgment on Jerusalem.
God used this divination for His own purposes. He uses even evil to accomplish His purposes (i.e. the witch of
Endor, 1 Samuel 28 and Balaam, Numbers 22-24)!

Special Topic: Magic

verses.zh: 在右手中拿着为耶路撒冷占卜的签，使他安设撞城锤，张口叫杀，扬声呐喊，筑垒造台，以撞城锤，攻打城门。
verses.en: Into his right hand[NOTE:1] comes the portent for Jerusalem—to set up battering rams, to give the signal[NOTE:2] for slaughter, to shout out the battle cry,[NOTE:3] to set up battering rams against the gates, to erect a siege ramp, and to build a siege wall.
notes: Or “on the right side,” i.e., the omen mark on the right side of the liver.
Heb “to open the mouth” for slaughter.
Heb “to raise up a voice in a battle cry.”
verses.commentary:
21:22 This verse has a series of INFINITIVE CONSTRUCTS that describes the
Babylonian commander's (possibly Nebuchadnezzar himself) orders (fulfills Ezek. 4:2)

- to set battering rams

- to open the mouth for slaughter (possibly, "war cry," which would form a four-part chiasm with #1,2,3,4; see Special Topic: Hebrew Poetry)

- to lift up the voice with a battle cry

- to set battering rams against the gates

- to cast up mounds

- to build a siege wall

For a good brief discussion of siege techniques see Roland de Vaux, Ancient Israel,
vol. 1, pp. 236-240.

verses.zh: 据那些曾起誓的犹大人看来，这是虚假的占卜；但巴比伦王要使他们想起罪孽，以致将他们捉住。」
verses.en: But those in Jerusalem[NOTE:1] will view it as a false omen. They have sworn solemn oaths,[NOTE:2] but the king of Babylon[NOTE:3] will accuse them of violations[NOTE:4] in order to seize them.[NOTE:5]
notes: Heb “they”; the referent (the people in Jerusalem) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
When the people of Judah realized the Babylonians’ intentions, they would object on grounds that they had made a treaty with the Babylonian king (see 17:13).
Heb “he”; the referent (the king of Babylon) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Or “iniquity.”
Heb “and he will remind of guilt to be captured.” The king would counter their objections by pointing out that they had violated their treaty with him (see 17:18), thus justifying their capture.
verses.commentary:
21:23 This describes the reaction of the people of Jerusalem (cf. TEV). They think they are safe because
of their political alliances (i.e. with Neo-Babylon or Egypt).

The "he" can refer to

- Ezekiel speaking for YHWH

- YHWH Himself

- the king of Neo-Babylon

Jerusalem is being judged because of her continuing covenant disobedience. Their God is
now fighting against them!

▣ "they have sworn solemn oaths" This is the Qal PASSIVE PARTICIPLE
and the NOUN of the same root (BDB 989, KB 1396) for emphasis.
The Septuagint omits this phrase altogether. However, it may refer to the political alliance that Judah had with Babylon (cf. Ezek. 17:13;
2 Chr. 36:13).

verses.zh: 主耶和华如此说：「因你们的过犯显露，使你们的罪孽被记念，以致你们的罪恶在行为上都彰显出来；又因你们被记念，就被捉住。
verses.en: “Therefore this is what the Sovereign Lord says: ‘Because you have brought up[NOTE:1] your own guilt by uncovering your transgressions and revealing your sins through all your actions, for this reason you will be taken by force.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “caused to be remembered.”

Heb “Because you have brought to remembrance your guilt when your transgressions are uncovered so that your sins are revealed in all your deeds—because you are remembered, by the hand you will be seized.”
verses.commentary:
21:24 YHWH states that Judah's

- iniquity (BDB 730) will be remembered (BDB 269, KB 269, Hiphil INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT)

- transgressions (BDB 833) will be uncovered (BDB 162, KB
191, Niphal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT)

- sins (BDB 305) will appear (BDB 906, KB 1157, Niphal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT)

- people have come to remembrance (BDB 269, KB 269, Niphal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT)

- people will be sieged (BDB 1074, KB 1779, Niphal IMPERFECT)

The three words used to describe rebellion against YHWH (i.e. iniquity, transgressions, and sins)
appear together in several texts (cf. Exod. 34:7; Lev. 16:21; Job 13:23; Ps. 32:5; Isa. 59:12; Dan. 9:24).
They form a summary triad.

Special Topic: Sin in the OT

verses.zh: 你这受死伤行恶的以色列王啊，罪孽的尽头到了，受报的日子已到。
verses.en: “‘As for you, profane and wicked prince of Israel,[NOTE:1] whose day has come, the time of final punishment,
notes: This probably refers to King Zedekiah.
verses.commentary:
21:25-26 Notice the different ways of referring to Zedekiah (Neo-Babylon's puppet king of Josiah's line).

- O slain (NKJV, "O profane")

- wicked one

- prince of Israel

Notice what will happen to him when his day (i.e. in the time of the iniquity of the end) has come.

- remove the turban ‒ BDB 693, KB 747, Hiphil IMPERATIVE

- take off the crown ‒ BDB 926, KB 1202, Hiphil IMPERATIVE

(Here, "turban" (BDB 857) and "crown" (BDB 742) are parallel. This is surprising because in every other place the turban
is for a priest. In many texts the office of king and High Priest are co-leaders [cf. Psalm 110;
Zech. 3, 4; 6:12-13; Heb. 4:14-5:10; 6:13-7:28]).

21:26b, 27b These two concluding remarks seem Messianic (cf. E. W. Hengstenberg, Christology of the Old Testament, pp. 683-687).
In context Ezek. 21:26b refers to Neo-Babylon, but when Ezek. 21:27b is brought in it appears to refer to Gen. 49:10 (i.e. Shiloh), see

- F. F. Bruce, Answers to Questions, p. 7

- Gleason Archer, Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties, pp. 107-108

- These two taken together would describe Jesus as a humble one (cf. Zech. 9:9) and of the line of David (cf. Ezek. 34:23-24; 37:24,25; Jer. 30:9; Hosea 3:5).

It is surely possible that this refers to Nebuchadnezzar II as YHWH's instrument of judgment on Judah, as Cyrus II is later
YHWH's instrument of release from exile and then restoration (cf. Isa. 44:28-45:1). As a Christian I must be careful of my biases which desire to
read the full New Testament revelation back into the Old Covenant in too many places (e.g. Christ in the tabernacle). He is surely in the OT, but
not on every page. Here (1) the royal line is the issue and a prediction of a future restoration is possible and also (2) the repeated use of the phrase
"whose day has come in the time of the punishment of the end" in Ezek. 21:25 and 29 implies an eschatological setting.

verses.zh: 主耶和华如此说：当除掉冠，摘下冕，景况必不再像先前；要使卑者升为高，使高者降为卑。
verses.en: this is what the Sovereign Lord says:Tear off the turban;[NOTE:1] take off the crown!Things must change.[NOTE:2] Exalt the lowly;bring low the exalted![NOTE:3]
notes: Elsewhere in the Bible the turban is worn by priests (Exod 28:4, 37, 39; 29:6; 39:28, 31; Lev 8:9; 16:4), but here a royal crown is in view.
Heb “This not this.”
Heb “the high one.”

verses.zh: 我要将这国倾覆，倾覆，而又倾覆；这国也必不再有，直等到那应得的人来到，我就赐给他。」
verses.en: A total ruin I will make it![NOTE:1] Indeed, this[NOTE:2] will not beuntil he comes to whom is the right, and I will give it[NOTE:3] to him.’[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “A ruin, a ruin, a ruin I will make it.” The threefold repetition of the noun “ruin” is for emphasis and draws attention to the degree of ruin that would take place. See IBHS 233 §12.5a and GKC 431-32 §133.k. The pronominal suffix (translated “it”) on the verb “make” is feminine in Hebrew. The probable antecedent is the “turban/crown” (both nouns are feminine in form) mentioned in verse 26. The point is that the king’s royal splendor would be completely devastated as judgment overtook his realm and brought his reign to a violent end.

The pronoun “this” is feminine, while the following negated verb (“will not be”) is masculine. Some emend the verb to a feminine form (see BHS), In this case the statement refers to the destiny of the king's turban crown (symbolizing his reign). See the previous note. It ultimately denotes kingship in Israel, as with “not this” in v. 26.

Horace D. Hummel, Ezekiel (Concordia Commentary), 2:642, states that the suffixed object of the Hebrew verb for “give” (נָתַן, natan) can be indirect: “to him,” while the direct object (“it”) is understood from the preceding “right.” However, a more likely candidate for the understood object would be “this,” the turban/crown and the kingship it implies. The one who comes already has the “right.”

A popular alternative view of this verse takes “right” as “judgment,” views the one who comes as Nebuchadnezzar, and translates “until” (עַד, ‘ad) as “when.” The basis for this unique translation of עַד (which rarely can mean “while”) is that here it would refer to the period during which the devastation is realized rather than to its termination point. See L. C. Allen, Ezekiel (WBC), 2:19, 21. Ezekiel often has מִשְׁפָּט as “judgment” and does not use it elsewhere as “right.” God promises to “give” “judgment” to the Babylonians in 23:24, as he would here. However, “right” is a normal sense for מִשְׁפָּט, and even most who see Nebuchadnezzar as the one who comes find an allusion to Gen 49:10 here, though inverted. However, this verse can alter the idea of Gen 49:10 even without Allen’s view, since Gen 49:10 promises that the scepter will not depart from Judah until the Messiah comes, while Ezek 21:27 promises that the royal turban/crown will be a ruin until Messiah comes. Robert W. Jenson, Ezekiel (Brazos Theological Commentary on the Bible), 173, favors the traditional view “because of the eschatological rhetoric of the whole poem,” adding that “ending merely with Nebuchadnezzar would be a poetically disastrous anticlimax.” For Ezek 34:23-24 and 37:22, 24-25 promise the restoration of Davidic kingship in the Messiah.tn Hummel, Ezekiel, 2:658, states that “very early” interpreters saw similarity between this verse and Gen 49:10. Early Christian scholars like Jerome interpreted Ezek 21:27 of Jesus Christ, as did the majority of Christian scholars until rather recent times. The phrase “until he comes to whom it belongs” in Gen 49:10 resembles the words here. “Until” and “comes” are the same in both verses. In both verses there follows a relative pronoun like “who,” the preposition “to,” a prepositional object “him,” and an understood linking verb “is.” An allusion would favor those Hebrew words having the same meaning in both verses, with “right, legal claim” as the sense for מִשְׁפָּט, (mishpat) rather than “judgment,” since it is more compatible with an allusion.
verses.commentary:
21:27 "A ruin, a ruin, a ruin" A threefold repetition is a Hebrew idiom expressing the superlative degree (cf. Isa. 6:3; Jer. 7:4). It
possibly links to Ezek. 21:14. The interpretive issue is to whom or what does the FEMININE form refer?

- the sword of the Lord

- the turban, crown, symbol of Davidic reign

Does this verse refer to the future fall of Babylon (v. 30) or to Zedekiah and Judah?

verses.zh: 「人子啊，要发预言说：主耶和华论到亚扪人和他们的凌辱，吩咐我如此说：有刀，有拔出来的刀，已经擦亮，为行杀戮，使他像闪电以行吞灭。
verses.en: “As for you, son of man, prophesy and say, ‘This is what the Sovereign Lord says concerning the Ammonites and their coming humiliation:[NOTE:1] “‘A sword, a sword drawn for slaughter,polished to consume,[NOTE:2] to flash like lightning—
notes: Heb “their reproach.”

Heb “to contain, endure,” from כוּל (khul). Since that sense is difficult here, most take the text to read either “to consume” or “for destruction.” GKC 186 §68.i suggests that the form represents the Hiphil of אָכַל (’akhal, “consume”). The ’alef (א) would have dropped out, as it sometimes does and might do with אָכַל in Ezek 42:5. D. I. Block (Ezekiel [NICOT], 1:693) prefers seeing כוּל as a byform of כָּלָה (kalah, “be complete”), with a meaning like “consume” in the Hiphil. The weakness of Block’s suggestion is that כָּלָה does not elsewhere exhibit a Hiphil.
verses.commentary:
21:28-32 This prophecy ("prophesy," BDB 612, KB 659, Niphal IMPERTIVE) is against the land of Ammon
(cf. Ezek. 21:20). It is for one of two possible reasons:

- It possibly relates to Ammon taking advantage, possibly even some participation in the fall, of Judah (as Edom did in chapter 35).

- God's sure justice on the iniquity of Ammon.

The flow of thought could be outlined as follows:

- Ammon, mentioned in Ezek. 21:20, will also be destroyed, Ezek. 21:28 (cf. Ezek. 25:1-7).

- This is happening because

- of their reproach (cf. Ezek. 36:15; Zeph. 2:8-10)

- of their false prophets' messages from their divinations, Ezek. 21:29 (i.e. Ezek. 21:30a; see
Special Topic: Diviner)

- they are wicked murderers, Ezek. 21:29

- their time has come, Ezek. 21:29

- How YHWH will judge (Ezek. 21:30) is specified in Ezek. 21:31-32.

- I shall pour out My indignation on you, Ezek. 21:31

- I shall blow on you with the fire of My wrath, Ezek. 21:31

- I shall give you into the hand of brutal men, skilled in destruction, Ezek. 21:31

- you will be fuel for the fire, Ezek. 21:32

- your blood will be in the midst of the land, Ezek. 21:32

- you will not be remembered, Ezek. 21:32

Another possible way to interpret these last three verses is to see them as referring to Neo-Babylon (i.e. YHWH's sword),
not Ammon (see Encyclopaedia Judaica, vol. 6, p. 1086). This would make sense of Ezek. 21:30a, "return it to its sheath." Neo-Babylon's
judgment was in the future. YHWH used her to judge His people (and other surrounding nations), but in return they were responsible for their own sin.
Cyrus II would be YHWH's sword to destroy them (cf. Isa. 44:28-45:1).

verses.zh: 人为你见虚假的异象，行谎诈的占卜，使你倒在受死伤之恶人的颈项上。他们罪孽到了尽头，受报的日子已到。
verses.en: while seeing false visions about you and reading lying omens about you[NOTE:1]—to place you[NOTE:2] on the necks of the profane wicked,[NOTE:3] whose day has come,the time of final punishment.
notes: Heb “in the seeing concerning you falsehood, in divining concerning you a lie.” This probably refers to the attempts of the Ammonites to ward off judgment through prophetic visions and divination.
The antecedent for you is the sword mentioned in v. 28.
The second half of the verse appears to state that the sword of judgment would fall upon the wicked Ammonites, despite their efforts to prevent it.

verses.zh: 你将刀收入鞘吧！在你受造之处、生长之地，我必刑罚你。
verses.en: Return it to its sheath![NOTE:1] In the place where you were created,[NOTE:2] in your native land, I will judge you.
notes: Once the Babylonian king’s sword (vv. 19-20) has carried out its assigned task, the Lord commands a halt. The resheathed sword will return to the land where it was created, and there itself face judgment. The pronouns continue to be second person feminine singular. The sword figuratively represents the Babylonian nation, whose land is the locus of judgment.

In the Hebrew text of vv. 30-32 the second person verbal and pronominal forms are generally feminine singular. This continues the address of the personified Babylonian sword from verse 29 (the Hebrew word for “sword” is feminine). “Return” is masculine, either due to the Hebrew preference for the masculine gender, or to the fact that soldiers were men.

verses.zh: 我必将我的恼恨倒在你身上，将我烈怒的火喷在你身上；又将你交在善于杀灭的畜类人手中。
verses.en: I will pour out my anger on you; the fire of my fury I will blow on you.I will hand you over to brutal men,who are skilled in destruction.[NOTE:1]
notes: The imagery of blowing on the sword with fire and putting it in the hands of skillful men can evoke the work of smithies.
verses.commentary: 21:31 "into the hand" See Special Topic: Hand

verses.zh: 你必当柴被火焚烧，你的血必流在国中，你必不再被记念，因为这是我―耶和华说的。」
verses.en: You will become fuel for the fire—your blood will stain the middle of the land;[NOTE:1] you will no longer be remembered,for I, the Lord, have spoken.’”
notes: Heb “your blood will be in the middle of the land.” sn This can be the blood that covered the sword in its great slaughter (v. 14), figuratively representing the end of Babylon. The pronouns are still second person feminine singular.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing

1And the word of the Lord came to me saying, 2"Son of man,
set your face toward Jerusalem, and speak against the sanctuaries and prophesy against the land of Israel; 3and say to the land of Israel, 'Thus says the
Lord, "Behold, I am against you; and I will draw My sword out of its sheath and cut off from you the righteous and the wicked. 4Because
I will cut off from you the righteous and the wicked, therefore My sword will go forth from its sheath against all flesh from south to north. 5Thus all flesh will
know that I, the Lord, have drawn My sword out of its sheath. It will not return to its sheath again."' 6As for you, son of man,
groan with breaking heart and bitter grief, groan in their sight. 7And when they say to you, 'Why do you groan?' you shall say, 'Because of the news that is coming;
